paragraphs.text: Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) is a pathologic condition where fetal growth is restrained by either extrinsic (maternal) fac tors or a disorder intrinsic to the fetus itself. Each year upwards of 30 million infants are born following IUGR worldwide [1]; rates are especially high in developing countries because of poor nutrition and limited prena tal care. This is a significant problem because of the morbidity that accompanies IUGR. Complications in the immediate post partum period include hypoglycemia, necro tizing enterocolitis, and persistence of the fetal circulation, to name a few [2]. Moreover, the first-year survival rate is substantially reduced in infants who have experienced IUGR [3, 4].
paragraphs.heading: 4.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: There are long-term sequelae of IUGR as well [5]. Affected children may have poor school performance and attenuated intellec tual development [6, 7]. There is evidence that intrauterine nutrient deprivation leads to obe sity, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia
paragraphs.heading: 4.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: later in life, an effect thought to be due to in utero “programming” of metabolic status [8, 9]. Postnatal growth is also affected adversely [10, 11]. Somewhere between 10% and 40% of children born following IUGR remain growth-retarded in childhood [12, 13]. Many never reach normal adult size [14]. The effect of IUGR on subsequent growth and its ame lioration by growth hormone (GH) therapy are the focus of this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: 4.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The percentage of newborns said to have had IUGR depends on the definition applied but generally is around 3% in the United States and 10% in developing countries. It is important to consider definitions used to define IUGR as they have some bearing on the interpretation of published reports [15]. Intrauterine growth retardation (or intrauter ine growth restriction) is a failure to grow at a normal rate in the in utero environment. Sequential measurements of fetal size in utero are becoming increasingly common and now allow IUGR to be documented with greater precision and the phase of pregnancy during which the growth aberration occurred defined [16]. The more commonly used term is small for gestational age (SGA), which is simply a statistical threshold defining low birth weight at the calculated gestational age. Typical lines of demarcation are −2 SDs or <3rd percen tile. Though newborns who fall below this are assumed to have had a period of IUGR, in some cases they simply represent the end of the normal spectrum of birth size. Similarly, infants may have experienced IUGR, espe cially in the last trimester, but have a birth weight that surpasses the minimal standards. These newborns may have other features of IUGR such as decreased subcutaneous tissue and hypoglycemia.
paragraphs.heading: 4.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The growth rate of a human is greatest during the prenatal period with a linear growth veloc ity of up to 60 cm/year, making this period
paragraphs.heading: 4.1.1 Normal Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: especially vulnerable to factors that affect the regulation of growth [17, 18]. Fetal growth is determined by a complex interaction of maternal, placental, and fetal factors involv ing genetic, epigenetic, and hormonal path ways. Epigenetic mechanisms are of particular interest as they control the function of the genome by regulating gene expression without altering the DNA nucleotide sequence. Epigenetic modifications are heritable at the cell level and influenced by the environment, thus providing a mechanism by which the pre natal environment may “program” the off spring to develop altered metabolic states such as obesity or diabetes [19]. Given the essential role of (epi)genetics and nutrition in
paragraphs.heading: 4.1.1 Normal Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: fetal growth and development, it is not sur prising that pathogenic variants in genes involved in cell division or differentiation can negatively affect fetal growth and may explain the absence of postnatal catch-up growth in some cases [20, 21]. Gene clusters involved in growth and regulated by epigenetic mecha nisms are found in chromosomal regions 11p.15.5, 7p11.2, 15q11-q13, 14q32, and 20q13.32 [22].
paragraphs.heading: 4.1.1 Normal Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: insulin secretion increases in response to fetal glycemia, acting mainly in the third trimester when fetal weight velocity peaks. The placenta produces both IGF1 and IGF2, which are secreted into the fetal circulation. The pla centa also expresses multiple IGFBPs, influ encing the bioavailability of IGFs in the fetus [21]. IGF1 and IGF2 can compensate, at least partially, for deficiency of each other [24–27]. The growth-promoting effects of the IGFs are principally mediated by the type I or IGF1 receptor, a homolog of the insulin receptor [26]. The IGF2 “receptor,” in contrast, serves as a clearance mechanism of IGF2 and thereby modulates tissue IGF2 abundance [28, 29]. During fetal life, the IGF system operates largely independently of GH, which has little influence on body size before birth in humans. Thereafter the influence of IGF2 declines, and IGF1, under the control of GH, becomes the dominant growth regulator of postnatal life. However, at midgestation a GH variant (GHV) secreted by the placenta appears in the maternal circulation. GHV stimulates lipolysis and gluconeogenesis, increases maternal blood glucose, which passes through the placenta to the fetus. GHV also stimulates the synthesis of maternal IGF- 1, which is able to cross the placental barrier.
paragraphs.heading: 4.1.1 Normal Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: The etiologies of IUGR are as varied as those for postnatal short stature but typically fall into one of three classes. Maternal factors that lead to IUGR include deprivation of oxy gen or nutrients (severe maternal malnutri tion, multiple gestation, cigarette smoking, and high-altitude living), infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis, and AIDS), and toxins (alco hol). Placental deficiency due to suboptimal
paragraphs.heading: 4.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: implantation site, placental undergrowth, infarction, or vascular anomalies such as vela mentous cord insertion and placental heman giomas can also lead to IUGR. Factors intrinsic to the fetus constitute the final clas sification and are exemplified by chromosome aneuploidy (Turner syndrome, trisomy 13 and 18) and specific genetic defects (for a review see Finken et al. [21]).
paragraphs.heading: 4.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: A deficiency of insulin secretion (such as that which occurs in pancreatic agenesis) or action (e.g., insulin receptor deficiency/lepre chaunism) severely impairs fetal growth and is a rare cause of IUGR [30]. More common fetal insults that produce IUGR are hypoxia and nutrient deprivation. Restriction of oxy gen or nutrients results in adaptive responses by the fetus which tend to preserve organ dif ferentiation and maturation at the expense of physical growth and energy stores (i.e., fat and glycogen). The insulin-like growth factor (IGF) axis is intimately involved in these adaptive responses.

There are important reasons for establishing a diagno sis; however, it should be emphasized that in many cases it is impossible to ascertain the precise cause of prenatal growth failure [21]. Since this chapter deals primarily with the use of rhGH in augmenting growth in such chil dren, the diagnostic discussion is directed toward determining whether rhGH therapy is warranted. The diagnostic approach is framed under several relevant questions. 1. Does the patient have a disorder that limits
paragraphs.heading: 4.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: After birth, most SGA newborns increase their growth velocity substantially and approx imately 85% eventually catch up in height [12, 57, 58]. However, there is a relationship between birth weight and stature that is main tained for several years during childhood, with patients being born especially small and remaining short on the average [14, 59].
paragraphs.heading: 4.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Patients generally present to the endocri nologist in one of two ways. The first is imme diately following birth when categorized as SGA. The questions that arise at this time relate to potential causes of IUGR and whether the patient will have normal growth thereafter. The extent of the evaluation will depend on the severity of growth retardation, the existence of concurrent medical condi tions or dysmorphic features, and whether the cause of IUGR is evident.

A more common presentation is that of the short child between the ages of 3 and 8 years. The child was born with a low birth weight and was expected to “catch up.” However, catch-up never occurred, and the child has had the same relative degree of short stature for many years. That is, when plotted on the growth chart, the trajectory seems to parallel the norm, just three to five SDS below average. The child has been otherwise healthy, and parents are concerned that the short stat ure will become increasingly problematic as the patient ages. They wonder whether any thing can be done to improve stature. It is not always evident that the persistent small size is related to a growth disorder that began prior to birth. Only by reviewing the birth weight and history of pregnancy and delivery does this information come to light.
2. Is the cause of IUGR obvious?
The causes of growth failure are many, as are the tests that can be applied to such patients. One should consider the likely possibilities and apply the diagnostic tests that are reason

paragraphs.text: both pre- and postnatal growth?
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Certain common endocrine disorders, such as hypothyroidism and GH defi ciency, have the most pronounced effects on postnatal growth. Even when the con dition is congenital, most are born within the normal range for length and weight. Thus, these diagnoses are usually elimi nated when prenatal growth restriction is prominent. The same applies to common, acquired causes of growth failure such as celiac disease. Patients who are born SGA without dysmorphic features and show catch-up growth during the first year do not require further evaluation. Patients being evaluated for IUGR who are still in the first few months of life should simply be tracked in terms of growth if they have no dysmorphic features, malformations, or suspicious symptoms. Most patients des tined to catch up will demonstrate increased growth velocity during the first 6 months of life and will have caught up by the end of the first year [12, 61, 62]. Patients who have shown no evidence of improved growth following birth need fur ther evaluation.
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: A careful history and physical exami nation can be very helpful in explaining IUGR. Maternal hypertension and poor weight gain during pregnancy suggest a maternal factor. Dysmorphic features in the baby imply that a syndrome associated with IUGR is present. Useful diagnostic tests for evaluating patients with IUGR
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: are listed in Box 4.1. A karyotype is par ticularly important for females because Turner syndrome is typically accompanied by mild prenatal growth restriction some times without the characteristic pheno type. Patients with dysmorphic features should have karyotyping as well or be con sidered for other specialized genetic tests with further evaluation by a geneticist/dys morphologist. It is particularly important to recognize Bloom and Fanconi syn dromes, recessive disorders associated with severe IUGR, and poor postnatal growth. These patients have increased chromo somal breakage and usually develop malignancies later in childhood. For these reasons, rhGH therapy may be contraindi cated. The diagnosis of Bloom syndrome is often suspected with routine chromo some studies in which there is increased chromosome breakage and formation of triradial chromosomes. Confirmation requires direct gene analysis.
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Assessment of renal function is required because mild forms of renal dys plasia can produce IUGR and moderate postnatal growth failure that is otherwise not evident. These patients may manifest oligohydramnios as a clue to the diagnosis. 3. Why has the patient not shown catch-up

paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: If more were known about the mecha nisms involved in catch-up growth, it would be easier to explain why, in certain cases, it does not occur. In some situations, the fetal growth retardation may have been so severe and the cellular mass at birth is so low that the overall somatic size is ulti mately restricted. Even with the normal ization of nutritional and hormonal factors, simply restoring normal growth (body size doubling at normal intervals) still leaves a person small relative to the peers. In other cases, patients do not reach normal size following birth because of the persistence of a defect in growth regula tion or cellular growth and replication. From a practical point of view, it is impor
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: tant to consider that catch-up growth may be impaired in patients whose nutritional status is compromised. A careful dietary history and review by a nutritionist can be helpful and is especially indicated in a patient with low weight for height.
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Abnormalities in the GH/IGF axis clearly explain the lack of catch-up in patients with molecular defects in IGF1, IGF2, and IGF1R. However, changes in the secretion and action of GH and the IGFs are also involved in the broader pop ulation of affected patients. Circulating concentrations of IGF-I tend to be rela tively low at birth in children born SGA and remain suppressed in those with poor catch-up [63]. Though the absence of GH clearly cannot explain their prenatal growth retardation, studies by Boguszewski et al. [64] and de Waal et al. [65] have sug gested that there is an increased incidence of low GH secretion in patients with short stature following IUGR. These data imply that reduced pituitary GH secretion con tributes to relatively poor postnatal growth in some cases. However, the ability of indi ces of GH secretion to predict response to GH therapy for this group of patients is not clear. Earlier reports suggested that low overnight GH concentrations or low IGF1 concentrations were associated with an improved response [66, 67], whereas later reports, examining greater numbers, found no predictive value in these mea sures [68–70]. However, such studies fre quently differ in the patient selection (e.g., severity of IUGR and short stature), the dosing of rhGH, and the tests of GH release. Studies that examine larger num bers of patients only slightly SGA likely include a significant proportion that does not necessarily have disorders of prenatal growth and/or have differing etiologies from those patients who are −4 to −5 SD below average for birth size. In addition, large doses of rhGH administered could obscure underlying differences in sensitiv ity to GH.
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: There is also evidence that short SGA children may have relative resistance to IGF1 [71]. Cutfield et al. [72] showed that circulating concentrations of IGF1, while lower than normal in short SGA children, were higher than those with idiopathic short stature of the same age. Chatelain et al. [73] demonstrated that short SGA children required higher circulating con centrations of IGF1 during GH treatment to achieve growth rates equal to children with GH deficiency or familial short stat ure treated with GH.
paragraphs.heading: 4.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Most patients do not meet the bio chemical criteria for classic GH deficiency or other known endocrine disorders. Thus, the most likely explanation for their poor postnatal growth is the persistence of a problem intrinsic to the fetus. There may be a specific genetic defect that continues to limit growth, or the early growth restric tion has, in some way, reprogrammed the growth regulating system so that the child remains small. The evidence above sug gests that the reprogramming involves alterations in the GH/IGF axis that result in a situation analogous to that seen with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 2 diabetes is characterized by insulin resistance cou pled with reduced insulin secretion. Thus, the short child born SGA could be thought of as having “type 2 growth deficiency,” where there are inadequate circulating lev els of IGF1 in the face of relative IGF resistance.

The main goals of rhGH treatment of the short children born SGA are to improve height during childhood and to achieve a final height adequate for the appropriate popula tion. As previously described, primary distur bances of GH/IGF are uncommon explanations for the lack of catch-up growth

paragraphs.text: However, the doses employed were modest by today’s standards, being similar to those given to patients with GH deficiency at the time. Subsequent studies showed clearly that rhGH stimulates growth in short children born SGA and that such growth can be sustained for sev eral years [85] increasing adult height ( Fig. 4.3). Meaningful gains require a dose higher than typical for GH deficiency over several years of treatment. Overall, an increase of about 2 SDS in height over the height SDS at treatment initiation can be expected when rhGH is given for 5 years or more [70]. However, the outcome is significantly influ enced by the timing of puberty. Catch-up growth that yields a normal height for age and sex before starting puberty is required to achieve the expected final height. Only modest gains in SDS occur in the absence of treat ment or when treatment starts close to puber tal onset [87, 88].
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.1 Effects on Skeletal Growth

paragraphs.text: Treatment should be limited to those patients in whom short stature is at least moderately severe (<2.0 SDS) and where there is little
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: expectation of meaningful catch-up growth over the next several years. If significant catch-up is going to occur, it is usually evident during the first year of life. Since growth pat terns can be variable, careful measures over at least 6 months (preferably 12) should be per formed to assess underlying growth velocity in all patients prior to treatment. Patients born at term that present after age 2 with persistent short stature typically have a growth rate in the low-normal range and are unlikely to show substantial improvement in height SDS over the next several years. For preterm SGA, the expected age for catch-up growth is 3 years of age.
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: Assessment of final height prognosis with a bone age measurement is not generally use ful in selecting those most likely to benefit from rhGH treatment. As most patients are quite young and may have underlying patho logical conditions, the prediction is usually inaccurate and overestimates final height [89].
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: Since younger patients respond better, treatment can be initiated once it is clear that the growth velocity is insufficient to normalize height. Patients in mid-childhood would likely benefit as well, but those well into puberty are at a disadvantage because of the limited time before epiphyseal fusion [87].
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: Few studies evaluate the growth response of patients with specific genetic syndromes in numbers sufficient to assess efficacy, with the exception is SRS. These patients, although typically shorter than the average SGA patient, show a growth response to rhGH equivalent to the nonsyndromic [90]. For other syndromic patients, in the absence of data to the contrary, it is reasonable to con sider that rhGH may also be effective and evaluate the response in each case.
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: Measures of GH secretion, though fre quently performed, do not appear to predict growth response and are not recommended unless the growth velocity is persistently reduced and signs of GH deficiency or hypo pituitarism are present [74]. The authors’ approach is to measure circulating IGF1 and IGFBP-3 and only perform tests of GH release if these parameters are subnormal or there are other reasons to suspect pituitary involvement. If the IGFs and measures of GH release are all low, this suggests a lack of GH is limiting the skeletal growth and the need for supplementation clear. Aboveaverage concentrations of IGF1 may signify IGF insensitivity in a child with both pre- and postnatal growth failure [33, 38, 39]. The diag nosis of GH deficiency should not alter the decision to treat, but IGF1 insensitivity will blunt the response. The purpose of studying GH/IGF1 axis is to individualize the clinical management of the patients.

Periodic assessment of circulating IGF1 during rhGH therapy is recommended for patients receiving rhGH to evaluate adher ence to treatment and as a safety approach. Doses of rhGH that produce supranormal circulating levels of IGF1 raise concerns regarding increased risk of severe adverse events, in particular risk of malignancies. The theory is reasonable, but unproven by the best-quality information available [95, 96]. In

paragraphs.text: addition, the measurement of IGF1 in the cir culation is affected by multiple factors that may complicate the interpretation [97].
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.3 rhGH Dosing and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: For short children born SGA, IGF1 levels may appear to be in the hazardous range while receiving rhGH, but it is possible that a degree of IGF1 resistance plays a role in growth limi tation. In that circumstance, raising IGF1 concentrations above normal might be needed, especially if the growth response is less than that desired [98]. Furthermore, the range of IGF1 blood levels is very wide among normal children suggesting varied sensitivity of individuals to IGF1 or that circulating IGF1 is a poor reflection of signal strength at the cellular level. In fact, titrating GH dose by circulating IGF1 in hopes of optimizing treat ment appears less effective than the standard dosing strategy [99, 100]. Clearly, more work needs to be done to define how biomarkers of GH action can be used in the selection of therapeutic regimens for patients [101]. In the meantime, a reasonable approach is to use rhGH in the dose ranges as outlined above, with adjustments to achieve growth rates yielding catch-up growth when the patient is below the 5th percentile for height and pre scribe rhGH at doses that will maintain nor mal growth when the patient is solidly in the normal range for height. With this approach circulating IGF1 levels are often within the
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.3 rhGH Dosing and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: upper normal range during the growth main tenance phase [102].
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.3 rhGH Dosing and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Short children born SGA may have reduced insulin sensitivity before the start of rhGH treatment [103]. Moreover, rhGH treat ment typically results in a further decrease in insulin sensitivity with a compensatory increase in insulin secretion due to the insulinantagonistic effects of GH [104–106]. However, rhGH therapy in short children born SGA rarely causes glucose intolerance or diabetes and metabolic parameters return to baseline or even improve following rhGH withdrawal [107]. Thus, there is no specific recommendation for monitoring glucose metabolism routinely except for patients with familial predisposition or obesity.
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.3 rhGH Dosing and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Monitoring adherence to the treatment regimen is essential. Poor adherence is one of the most common factors underlying subopti mal growth during rhGH therapy and should be actively evaluated and managed before considering other illnesses that can affect growth, unresponsiveness, or an increment of dose. Improving families’ adherence to rhGH treatment is required to achieve the expected efficacy and promote pharmacoeconomy [108, 109].
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.3 rhGH Dosing and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Patients should have re-evaluation at a minimum of 6 months intervals with careful history and physical examination, seeking

paragraphs.text: signs and symptoms of scoliosis, other ortho pedic abnormalities, intracranial hyperten sion, and assessment of growth response to therapy. It is worth performing a bone age around the age of 8 years and regularly from the onset of puberty onwards [80]. This method is inaccurate in predicting adult height in children born SGA [74].
paragraphs.heading: 4.5.3 rhGH Dosing and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: As pubertal development has a great impact on final height, pubertal onset and progress need to be carefully monitored in SGA patients. The pattern of puberty in chil dren born SGA is heterogenous, with a sub group characterized by either early onset, shorter or earlier peak height velocity, and/or accelerated bone maturation [110, 111]. The combination of rhGH and gonadotropinreleasing hormone analog treatment in SGA children whose final height may be compro mised because of a significant growth deficit at the pubertal onset can be considered [112].

Despite the known individual response to treatment, there are recognizable factors asso ciated with an improved outcome such as younger age and greater height at the start of treatment, height gain during the first year of treatment, longer duration of treatment, length at birth, higher parental height, and delayed bone age for chronological age. Moreover, the underlying etiology of SGA also impacts the response to the treatment [74].
paragraphs.heading: 4.6 Outcomes

paragraphs.text: After two decades of follow up of SGA patients treated with rhGH, benefits of rhGH
paragraphs.heading: 4.6 Outcomes

paragraphs.text: treatment beyond stature have been observed. There is an improvement in body composition (i.e., a decrease in fat mass and an increase in lean body mass) due to the lipolytic and ana bolic effects of GH [104, 114, 115]. Positive effects on bone are reported as well with incre ments in bone mineral density [116] reflecting the significant role of the GH–IGF1 axis in the accrual of bone mass. Additionally, longterm GH treatment improves psychosocial development and health-related quality of life in children and adolescents born SGA [117, 118].
paragraphs.heading: 4.6 Outcomes

paragraphs.text: In summary, the efficacy of rhGH therapy is dependent upon making the correct diagno sis, starting treatment at an opportune time, administering the appropriate dose of rhGH, and maintaining patient adherence.
paragraphs.heading: 4.6 Outcomes

paragraphs.text: An important issue facing a physician pre scribing any drug is the possibility of adverse effects. Safety issues during rhGH replace ment may be related to the substance itself, to the formulation of the drug (impurities and additives), or the result of the genuine (nor mal) effects (growth of bones or other tissues, and metabolic actions). They may be also due to inappropriate doses or a true incompatibil ity with the patient being treated [119]. After many years of rhGH treatment in a large number of children, it is evident that rhGH rarely causes serious morbidity [120]. However, the short children born SGA deserves special consideration. First, the dose of rhGH prescribed is higher than that used for GH deficiency, and second, this patient population may have unique susceptibilities to certain pharmacological properties of GH.
paragraphs.heading: 4.7 Safety

paragraphs.text: Epidemiological and experimental data indicate that humans born SGA have an increased incidence of obesity and type 2 dia betes as adults, with the implication that a period of fetal undernutrition results in a resetting of intrinsic insulin sensitivity [121, 122]. Individuals who had IUGR show evi dence of decreased insulin sensitivity already as children [123]. Could increased levels of
paragraphs.heading: 4.7 Safety

paragraphs.text: GH, which diminish insulin sensitivity, add to the risk of developing obesity, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance later in life? Thus far data from patients treated show only modest effects on basal insulin levels [124] and no clinically significant impact on glucose or lipid metabolism [114]. Moreover, measures of carbohydrate metabolism after the comple tion of rhGH treatment are no different in those treated compared to untreated adults born SGA. If anything, lipid profiles and blood pressure indices are better in those treated [125]. Nonetheless, the number of patients treated with the highest doses remains too few to detect uncommon, but significant, long-term sequelae.
paragraphs.heading: 4.7 Safety

paragraphs.text: The known pro-proliferative, angiogenic, and anti-apoptotic properties of GH and IGF1 have raised concerns regarding a possi ble increased risk of malignancy [126, 127] though this has been difficult to quantify. Analyses of the risk of rhGH treatment in patients who developed GH deficiency as a consequence of tumor treatment do not sug gest a role for GH in the development of a relapse [127–129]. However, large epidemio logical studies find that the risks for prostate cancer [130] and breast cancer [131] are increased for people with serum IGF1 con centrations in the upper ranges of normal. The studies do not prove cause and effect, but tumor cells in culture frequently express IGF1 receptors and replicate in response to IGF1 [132]. This raises the question as to whether the high IGF1 levels that generally accom pany high-dose rhGH therapy might increase the risk for neoplasia over the long term. Thus, rhGH treatment is usually contraindi cated in children with cancer predisposition syndromes (e.g., Bloom syndrome, Li Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Fanconi anemia). However, it may be cau tiously considered in those with proven GH deficiency and only after informed discussion with the patient and parents/guardians [127]. Despite the above concerns, review by interna tional pediatric endocrinology societies con clude that rhGH can be safely administered to children without known risk factors for malig nancy [74, 133].
paragraphs.heading: 4.7 Safety

paragraphs.text: Most published studies of rhGH safety in children focused on short- or intermediateterm events. Only recently has it been possible to begin to assess late effects in adults who were treated with rhGH during childhood for nongrowth hormone-deficient conditions such as the short children born SGA. SAGhE (Safety and Appropriateness of Growth Hormone Treatments in Europe) is an ongo ing large, epidemiologic study (n = approx. 24,000, with more than 400,000 patient-years of follow-up) that examines long-term outcomes of treatment [134, 135]. Initial reports suggested that all-cause mortality and stroke were increased in adults treated with rhGH in childhood and that the risk may increase with higher doses, at least for mortal ity [136, 137]. However, the number of adverse events detected was very low, the appropriate ness of reference populations challenged, and results not yet confirmed. Thus, a recent, society-sponsored, position paper concluded “the aggregate evidence from available data sets does not support an association between ongoing or previous rhGH therapy and allcause mortality” [98].
paragraphs.heading: 4.7 Safety

paragraphs.text: Savendahl et al. classified pediatric patients treated with rhGH into three risk groups based on diagnosis and considered the short children born SGA as a low-risk group. They analyzed individuals born SGA separately, showing that the risk of serious adverse effects is very low in individuals without predisposing risk factors, and there was no indication that rhGH therapy caused new malignancies or

diabetes. On the contrary, short children born SGA with obesity, accelerated catch-up growth and/or familial diabetes are considered a subgroup with a higher risk of metabolic disorder in the long-term follow-up [134].

Finally, additional complications described for rhGH therapy, include orthope dic problems such as scoliosis (inci dence—148/100,000) and slipped capital femoral epiphysis (15–19/100,000), especially in obese children and secondary intracranial hypertension (81/100,000) [138].

Most patients without GH deficiency should cease rhGH treatment when near adult height is achieved, defined as growth velocity below 2 cm/year and/or bone maturation above 14 years in girls and 16 years in boys. The rationale for timely suspension lies in avoiding unnecessary exposure to rhGH when it no longer stimulates growth, preventing the occurrence of acromegaloid changes, and reducing cost. Treatment should be discontin ued or interrupted before adult height attain ment when the growth response is poor (height velocity <−1 SDS/age and sex), there is a severe adverse event, or a diagnosis is uncov ered with a high risk of malignancy [74].

Presently there is no indication for con tinuing rhGH after epiphyseal closure. However, recent guidelines recommend that previously rhGH-treated young adults born SGA should maintain or adopt a healthy diet and lifestyle with regular exercise to avoid excessive weight gain in order to prevent met abolic and/or cardiovascular disease [74].

There are many reasons why a child is born SGA; at least half the time, the cause is not evident. Nevertheless, 80–90% of the children will show improved growth after birth and reach heights in the normal range by age 2 years. For those that remain short, stature below the 3rd percentile is likely to persist. Growth hormone treatment is effective at stimulating growth and improving adult height and is generally safe. Tests of growth hormone
paragraphs.heading: 4.8 Summary

paragraphs.text: secretion and action are typically not helpful in making specific diagnoses or predicting the response to treatment in this population. Careful monitoring during treatment and attention to appropriate dosing are important because responses are variable. Some patients will not respond sufficiently, and treatment is unlikely to benefit them. Advances in our abil ity to make specific diagnoses using molecular genetic techniques will likely improve our abil ity to establish causes of IUGR and determine appropriate treatment regimens.

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_4 ## PDF page 113 | printed page 96 Key Points 5 Intrauterine growth retardation is caused by a variety of conditions that affect the offspring in multiple ways. 5 Most individuals born small for gesta tional age (SGA) show catch-up growth by age 2 years for those born at term and by 3 years for the preterm and reach a normal adult height. 5 For those who do not show catch-up ### 4 growth, growth hormone treatment accelerates growth and increases stat ure, but the responses are variable. 5 The dose of growth hormone used to treat the short children born SGA is more than that used for growth hor mone deficiency. 5 Treatment at relatively young ages yields an improved response. ### 4.1 Introduction Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) is a pathologic condition where fetal growth is restrained by either extrinsic (maternal) fac tors or a disorder intrinsic to the fetus itself. Each year upwards of 30 million infants are born following IUGR worldwide [1]; rates are especially high in developing countries because of poor nutrition and limited prena tal care. This is a significant problem because of the morbidity that accompanies IUGR. Complications in the immediate post partum period include hypoglycemia, necro tizing enterocolitis, and persistence of the fetal circulation, to name a few [2]. Moreover, the first-year survival rate is substantially reduced in infants who have experienced IUGR [3, 4]. There are long-term sequelae of IUGR as well [5]. Affected children may have poor school performance and attenuated intellec tual development [6, 7]. There is evidence that intrauterine nutrient deprivation leads to obe sity, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia later in life, an effect thought to be due to in utero “programming” of metabolic status [8, 9]. Postnatal growth is also affected adversely [10, 11]. Somewhere between 10% and 40% of children born following IUGR remain growth-retarded in childhood [12, 13]. Many never reach normal adult size [14]. The effect of IUGR on subsequent growth and its ame lioration by growth hormone (GH) therapy are the focus of this chapter. The percentage of newborns said to have had IUGR depends on the definition applied but generally is around 3% in the United States and 10% in developing countries. It is important to consider definitions used to define IUGR as they have some bearing on the interpretation of published reports [15]. Intrauterine growth retardation (or intrauter ine growth restriction) is a failure to grow at a normal rate in the in utero environment. Sequential measurements of fetal size in utero are becoming increasingly common and now allow IUGR to be documented with greater precision and the phase of pregnancy during which the growth aberration occurred defined [16]. The more commonly used term is small for gestational age (SGA), which is simply a statistical threshold defining low birth weight at the calculated gestational age. Typical lines of demarcation are −2 SDs or <3rd percen tile. Though newborns who fall below this are assumed to have had a period of IUGR, in some cases they simply represent the end of the normal spectrum of birth size. Similarly, infants may have experienced IUGR, espe cially in the last trimester, but have a birth weight that surpasses the minimal standards. These newborns may have other features of IUGR such as decreased subcutaneous tissue and hypoglycemia. ### 4.1.1 Normal Fetal Growth The growth rate of a human is greatest during the prenatal period with a linear growth veloc ity of up to 60 cm/year, making this period ## PDF page 114 | printed page 97 especially vulnerable to factors that affect the regulation of growth [17, 18]. Fetal growth is determined by a complex interaction of maternal, placental, and fetal factors involv ing genetic, epigenetic, and hormonal path ways. Epigenetic mechanisms are of particular interest as they control the function of the genome by regulating gene expression without altering the DNA nucleotide sequence. Epigenetic modifications are heritable at the cell level and influenced by the environment, thus providing a mechanism by which the pre natal environment may “program” the off spring to develop altered metabolic states such as obesity or diabetes [19]. Given the essential role of (epi)genetics and nutrition in 21 fetal growth and development, it is not sur prising that pathogenic variants in genes involved in cell division or differentiation can negatively affect fetal growth and may explain the absence of postnatal catch-up growth in some cases [20, 21]. Gene clusters involved in growth and regulated by epigenetic mecha nisms are found in chromosomal regions 11p.15.5, 7p11.2, 15q11-q13, 14q32, and 20q13.32 [22]. 4.1 23 ## PDF page 115 | printed page 98 insulin secretion increases in response to fetal glycemia, acting mainly in the third trimester when fetal weight velocity peaks. The placenta produces both IGF1 and IGF2, which are secreted into the fetal circulation. The pla centa also expresses multiple IGFBPs, influ encing the bioavailability of IGFs in the fetus [21]. IGF1 and IGF2 can compensate, at least partially, for deficiency of each other [24–27]. The growth-promoting effects of the IGFs are principally mediated by the type I or IGF1 receptor, a homolog of the insulin receptor [26]. The IGF2 “receptor,” in contrast, serves as a clearance mechanism of IGF2 and thereby modulates tissue IGF2 abundance [28, 29]. During fetal life, the IGF system operates largely independently of GH, which has little influence on body size before birth in humans. Thereafter the influence of IGF2 declines, and IGF1, under the control of GH, becomes the dominant growth regulator of postnatal life. However, at midgestation a GH variant (GHV) secreted by the placenta appears in the maternal circulation. GHV stimulates lipolysis and gluconeogenesis, increases maternal blood glucose, which passes through the placenta to the fetus. GHV also stimulates the synthesis of maternal IGF- 1, which is able to cross the placental barrier. ### 4 ### 4.2 Etiology The etiologies of IUGR are as varied as those for postnatal short stature but typically fall into one of three classes. Maternal factors that lead to IUGR include deprivation of oxy gen or nutrients (severe maternal malnutri tion, multiple gestation, cigarette smoking, and high-altitude living), infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis, and AIDS), and toxins (alco hol). Placental deficiency due to suboptimal implantation site, placental undergrowth, infarction, or vascular anomalies such as vela mentous cord insertion and placental heman giomas can also lead to IUGR. Factors intrinsic to the fetus constitute the final clas sification and are exemplified by chromosome aneuploidy (Turner syndrome, trisomy 13 and 18) and specific genetic defects (for a review see Finken et al. [21]). A deficiency of insulin secretion (such as that which occurs in pancreatic agenesis) or action (e.g., insulin receptor deficiency/lepre chaunism) severely impairs fetal growth and is a rare cause of IUGR [30]. More common fetal insults that produce IUGR are hypoxia and nutrient deprivation. Restriction of oxy gen or nutrients results in adaptive responses by the fetus which tend to preserve organ dif ferentiation and maturation at the expense of physical growth and energy stores (i.e., fat and glycogen). Safety issues during rhGH replace ment may be related to the substance itself, to the formulation of the drug (impurities and additives), or the result of the genuine (nor mal) effects (growth of bones or other tissues, and metabolic actions). They may be also due to inappropriate doses or a true incompatibil ity with the patient being treated [119]. After many years of rhGH treatment in a large number of children, it is evident that rhGH rarely causes serious morbidity [120]. However, the short children born SGA deserves special consideration. First, the dose of rhGH prescribed is higher than that used for GH deficiency, and second, this patient population may have unique susceptibilities to certain pharmacological properties of GH. Epidemiological and experimental data indicate that humans born SGA have an increased incidence of obesity and type 2 dia betes as adults, with the implication that a period of fetal undernutrition results in a resetting of intrinsic insulin sensitivity [121, 122]. Individuals who had IUGR show evi dence of decreased insulin sensitivity already as children [123]. Could increased levels of GH, which diminish insulin sensitivity, add to the risk of developing obesity, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance later in life? Thus far data from patients treated show only modest effects on basal insulin levels [124] and no clinically significant impact on glucose or lipid metabolism [114]. Moreover, measures of carbohydrate metabolism after the comple tion of rhGH treatment are no different in those treated compared to untreated adults born SGA. If anything, lipid profiles and blood pressure indices are better in those treated [125]. Nonetheless, the number of patients treated with the highest doses remains too few to detect uncommon, but significant, long-term sequelae. The known pro-proliferative, angiogenic, and anti-apoptotic properties of GH and IGF1 have raised concerns regarding a possi ble increased risk of malignancy [126, 127] though this has been difficult to quantify. Analyses of the risk of rhGH treatment in patients who developed GH deficiency as a consequence of tumor treatment do not sug gest a role for GH in the development of a relapse [127–129]. However, large epidemio logical studies find that the risks for prostate cancer [130] and breast cancer [131] are increased for people with serum IGF1 con centrations in the upper ranges of normal.
